{
  "body": "Properties of Matter: 1. When you pump air into a ball, the air takes up space and the ball gets a little heavier, so air has mass. 2. How easily heat or electricity moves through a material; the text says, \"Does heat or electricity move through it easily? That property is called conductivity.\" 3. Any two: hardness, whether a magnet pulls on it, conductivity, solubility. 4. Physical: \"In a physical change, like melting ice or dissolving salt, the material is still the same substance.\" 5. Any two: a new color, a gas, heat or light given off. 6. 265 grams; the total mass stays the same when matter changes, so 250 + 15 = 265.\nDoes Temperature Change How Fast Sugar Dissolves?: A strong hypothesis is testable and gives a reason (for example, warm water will dissolve sugar faster because its particles move faster). A fair test changes only the water temperature and keeps the cup, the amount of water, the amount of sugar and the stirring the same, with more than one trial. Data are recorded in °C and seconds; typical results show the warmest water dissolving the sugar fastest. The conclusion names the numbers (for example, 28 s at 45 °C against 95 s at 10 °C) and says whether the hypothesis was supported.\nMatter Check: 1. Chemical change; evidence: it fizzed and bubbled (a gas formed, which puffed up the bag) and the bag felt cold (a temperature change). 2. 280 grams before and 280 grams after; mass is conserved: the matter changed into new substances, but none was lost or added. 3. 280 g = 0.28 kg, because 1 kg = 1,000 g and 280 ÷ 1,000 = 0.28. 4. Less than 280 grams: the gas escapes from the open bag into the air, so it is not weighed. The matter still exists; it is just not on the scale. 5. Sample A; any two of: a magnet pulls on it, electricity flows through it, it is shiny. 6. Add water and stir: Sample B dissolves and the sand does not. Pour the mixture through a filter (or a paper towel) to catch the sand, then let the water evaporate to get Sample B back.\nScoring tip: for question 4, \"less\" with the reason that gas escapes is Proficient on reasoning; adding that the mass of the matter itself did not change is Advanced.",

files.codex/u1-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Matter.

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Air, water, sugar and you are all matter.

When sugar dissolves in water, it seems to disappear, but it is still there. The water gets sweeter, and the mass of the cup does not change!

In this unit we will:
- describe materials by their properties,
- tell a physical change from a chemical change,
- run a fair test of what makes sugar dissolve faster,
- show that the total mass stays the same when matter changes.",
  "id": "u1-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Everything Is Made of Matter",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students read informational text about properties of matter, quoting accurately and explaining science words from context (RI.5.1, RI.5.4).
- Students plan and carry out a fair test of dissolving, record data with units and use the data to explain a result (W.5.7, W.5.8).
- Students explain the relationship between a change in matter and its mass, and convert grams to kilograms (RI.5.3, 5.MD.A.1).

MATERIALS
- Clear cups, a measuring cup or graduated cylinder, sugar, measuring spoons, a thermometer in °C, a timer, spoons for stirring
- Cold, room-temperature and warm (not hot) tap water
- A digital scale in grams, a zip bag, baking soda, vinegar and a small cup for the teacher demonstration
- A magnet, a simple circuit tester, and samples to sort (paper clip, salt, sand, a glass marble)
- Safety goggles for every student

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Everything Is Made of Matter. Pump up a ball on the scale to show that air has mass. Lesson: Properties of Matter, read in pairs; discuss question 6 together.
Day 2: Properties stations: test the samples with a magnet, the circuit tester and a cup of water, and record each property in a table.
Day 3: Assignment: Does Temperature Change How Fast Sugar Dissolves? Groups write a hypothesis, decide what stays the same (cup, amount of water, amount of sugar, stirring) and what changes (temperature), then run three trials.
Day 4: Finish the investigation and write conclusions that quote the data. Demonstrate the sealed bag test and record the mass before and after. Practice converting grams to kilograms on a place-value chart.
Day 5: Assessment: Matter Check. Students read and answer on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a fair-test planner with three boxes (change, keep the same, measure) and a data table with the units already written in. Pre-teach property, dissolve and conserve with pictures.
- Support: read the assessment passage aloud to any student whose reading plan allows it; the answers stay their own.
- Stretch: ask students to design a second test of dissolving (stirring or grain size) and predict the result with a reason.
- Multilingual learners: post a word wall with pictures for mass, property, magnet, dissolve, gas and change. Let students explain their results with gestures and the frames first, then write.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit, your child is a materials scientist. We are describing matter by its properties, running a fair test to see whether warm or cold water dissolves sugar faster, and finding out that mass never disappears, even when sugar seems to vanish. At home, ask your child to show you a physical change (ice melting) and to tell you what stays the same.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Matter and Its Properties",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u2-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Where Is Earth's Water?: 1. About 97 hold salt water; 3 hold fresh water. 2. Frozen in glaciers and ice caps: \"About 2 of the 3 buckets would be frozen in glaciers and ice caps.\" 3. Water stored in soil and in tiny spaces between rocks underground. 4. When ocean water evaporates, the salt is left behind, so the water vapor and the rain it makes are fresh. 5. To make a huge amount of water easier to picture and compare: you can see that 97 out of 100 is almost all of it. 6. Main idea 1: most of Earth's water is salty or frozen, so very little is easy-to-use fresh water (detail: lakes, rivers and clouds fill only a few cupfuls). Main idea 2: the water cycle keeps making fresh water (detail: evaporation leaves the salt behind).\nExplain the Water Cycle: The drawing labels evaporation (the sun warms water and it rises as vapor), condensation (the vapor cools into drops that form clouds), precipitation (drops fall as rain, snow or hail) and collection (water gathers in oceans, lakes, rivers and the ground), with arrows showing the cycle. A strong spoken explanation follows the steps in order, says what causes each one (the sun's heat; cooling as the vapor rises; drops getting heavy) and says how the cycle starts again.\nWater Check: A strong explanation includes, in order: the sun warms the ocean and the drop evaporates into water vapor, leaving the salt behind; the vapor rises, cools and condenses into a cloud; the cloud moves over a mountain where it is cold, and the drop falls as snow (precipitation); the snow piles up and is pressed into glacier ice over many years (collection); later the ice melts, and the water flows downhill in a stream or river (runoff) back to the ocean. It is fresh because salt does not evaporate with the water.\nScoring tip: an explanation that names all four steps but never says what causes them is Developing on science; score organization on the order of the steps and the linking words, not on length.",

files.codex/u2-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Where does rain come from?

Water moves in a cycle:
1. Evaporation: the sun warms water and it rises as water vapor.
2. Condensation: the vapor cools into tiny drops that make clouds.
3. Precipitation: the drops fall as rain, snow or hail.
4. Collection: water gathers in oceans, lakes and the ground.

In this unit we will also find out where all of Earth's water is. Most of it is salty, and most of the fresh water is frozen!",
  "id": "u2-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "The Water Cycle",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students quote accurately from an informational text, find two main ideas and explain science words from context (RI.5.1, RI.5.2, RI.5.4).
- Students explain the water cycle aloud in a logical sequence, using a labeled drawing as a visual display (SL.5.4, SL.5.5).
- Students write an informative explanation of the water cycle with linking words and precise science vocabulary (W.5.2, W.5.4).

MATERIALS
- 100 paper cups (or 100 squares on a grid) to model Earth's water, with 97 colored blue for ocean, 2 white for ice and 1 for groundwater, lakes and rivers
- A clear bowl, plastic wrap, a small cup, warm water, salt and an ice cube for a water-cycle model
- Drawing paper, colored pencils, and devices to record the spoken explanation

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Water Cycle. Set up the bowl model: salty warm water in the bowl, an empty cup in the middle, plastic wrap on top with an ice cube over the cup. Predict what will happen.
Day 2: Check the model: water collects in the cup. Let a drop from the cup and a drop from the bowl dry on dark paper: only the bowl's drop leaves salt behind (no tasting in the lab). Lesson: Where Is Earth's Water? Build the 100-cup model.
Day 3: Assignment: Explain the Water Cycle. Students draw and label their drawing, then practice telling it to a partner using the frames.
Day 4: Students record their explanations. Partners give one star (what was clear) and one step (what to add, such as what makes vapor cool).
Day 5: Assessment: Water Check. Students write on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a cycle organizer with four arrows and the step names; let students tell their explanation before writing it.
- Support: offer a word bank for the assessment (evaporate, water vapor, condense, precipitation, glacier, melt, runoff).
- Stretch: ask students to add where a drop might spend a very long time (a glacier or deep groundwater) and why.
- Multilingual learners: label the drawing in English and the home language. Let students rehearse the spoken explanation with a partner who shares their language before recording in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are studying Earth's water. Did you know that if all of Earth's water filled 100 buckets, only about 3 would be fresh, and 2 of those would be frozen? Your child is learning how the water cycle keeps fresh water coming. Next time it rains, or a puddle dries up, ask your child to tell you where the water came from and where it is going.",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Earth's Water",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Four Spheres That Work Together: 1. Geosphere: rock, soil, sand and melted rock deep below; hydrosphere: all of Earth's water; atmosphere: the layer of air around Earth; biosphere: every living thing. 2. Wind picks up sand that hits rock again and again and wears it into new shapes (weathering). 3. Roots grow into cracks and split rocks apart; roots also hold soil in place so less washes away. 4. Weathering is the wearing away or breaking of rock in place; erosion is moving rock and soil from one place to another. 5. Example: rain (hydrosphere) falls on the bare hill (geosphere) and carries soil downhill (erosion); with no plants (biosphere) to hold it, more soil is lost. 6. Cause and effect: each paragraph tells how one sphere causes a change in another, for example wind causes weathering, water freezing causes cracks to widen.\nErosion on a Hill: A testable hypothesis gives a reason (for example, a steeper hill will lose more soil because the water runs faster). A fair test changes only the height and keeps the soil, the amount of water and the pouring the same, with more than one trial at each height. Data are in centimeters and grams. Typical results: soil washed off goes up as the height goes up, so the graphed points rise from left to right. Grass would hold the soil and reduce the loss. Spheres: the hydrosphere (water) erodes the geosphere (soil); plants would add the biosphere.\nEarth's Systems Check: 1. The atmosphere: ash shot into the sky, blocked sunlight, made towns dark at noon and made the air cooler. 2. Hot rock and gas melted the snow; the meltwater mixed with ash and soil to make mudflows that rushed into rivers, turned them brown and made them flood. 3. Harmed: the forest was knocked flat and buried, and many plants died. Helped: the ash broke down into mineral-rich soil, and new plants grew, then insects, birds and deer returned. 4. Example: hot rock from the volcano (geosphere) melted the snow (hydrosphere), and the mudflows buried the forest (biosphere). 5. Sand, mud and ash carried by water: \"a layer of sediment, the sand, mud and ash carried by the water.\" 6. Yes: atmosphere (ash cloud blocked sunlight and cooled the air), geosphere (hot rock poured down; ash became new soil), hydrosphere (snow melted; rivers flooded), biosphere (forest buried; plants and animals returned).\nScoring tip: on question 4, a chain that names three spheres but does not show how each event causes the next is Developing on reasoning.",
  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Earth's Systems",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Earth has four big systems, called spheres:
- Geosphere: rock, soil and sand, and the hot rock deep inside Earth.
- Hydrosphere: all of Earth's water, in oceans, rivers, ice and the ground.
- Atmosphere: the air around Earth.
- Biosphere: all living things, including you.

The spheres are always working together. Rain (hydrosphere) washes soil (geosphere) down a hill. Wind (atmosphere) blows sand that wears away rock. Tree roots (biosphere) hold the soil in place.

In this unit we will test how the steepness of a hill changes how much soil rain carries away.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Four Spheres, One Planet",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how events in Earth's spheres are connected, using cause and effect, and describe how a text is structured (RI.5.3, RI.5.5).
- Students explain science words from context and quote accurately when explaining a text (RI.5.4, RI.5.1).
- Students carry out a short investigation of erosion, record data and graph their results as points on a coordinate grid (W.5.7, W.5.8, 5.G.A.2).
- Students explain how an author uses evidence to support a point (RI.5.8).

MATERIALS
- Plastic trays or foil pans, sandy soil, blocks or books to raise one end, a ruler in centimeters
- A watering can or a cup with holes poked in the bottom, a measuring cup, a container to catch runoff
- A scale in grams (dry the collected soil on a paper plate overnight, or weigh it wet and say so)
- Grid paper for graphing; optional: a tray of soil with grass seed planted two weeks earlier

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Four Spheres, One Planet. Sort picture cards (a cloud, a fish, a cliff, a tree, the wind) into the four spheres. Lesson: Four Spheres That Work Together, read in pairs.
Day 2: Assignment: Erosion on a Hill. Groups write a hypothesis, build the hill, and run trials at three heights (for example 5, 10 and 15 cm), using the same amount of water each time.
Day 3: Weigh the dried soil and finish the data table. Mini-lesson on plotting points: the x-axis is hill height, the y-axis is soil washed off. Students graph and describe the pattern. Show the grassy tray if you have one.
Day 4: Build a class web showing how one storm affects all four spheres, then finish conclusions. Keep When the Mountain Woke Up unseen: it is the assessment's new text.
Day 5: Assessment: Earth's Systems Check. Students read and answer on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a cause-and-effect organizer (Because ___ happened in the ___, ___ happened in the ___). Pre-label the axes on the grid paper.
- Support: read the assessment passage aloud to any student whose reading plan allows it.
- Stretch: ask students to design a way to protect the hill (plants, rocks, terraces) and test it against a bare hill.
- Multilingual learners: post a four-sphere chart with pictures. Teach weathering and erosion with a gesture each (rubbing for weathering, carrying for erosion).

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning about Earth's four systems: land, water, air and living things, and how they change each other. This week your child is testing how rain carries soil down a hill. On a walk, look for evidence together: a muddy puddle at the bottom of a slope, roots holding a bank in place, or a crack in a sidewalk where a plant is growing.",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Earth's Systems",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u4-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Energy Moves Through an Ecosystem: 1. The sun. 2. From the air and water: \"most of the material in a giant oak came from the air and water.\" 3. A living thing, such as a fungus, bacterium or earthworm, that breaks down dead plants and animals; it returns minerals to the soil so plants can use them again, and without it dead matter would pile up and plants would run out of minerals. 4. \"Is eaten by\": the grass is eaten by the rabbit, and the rabbit is eaten by the fox; energy and matter move in the direction of the arrows. 5. Deer: herbivore; owl: carnivore; bear: omnivore; mushroom: decomposer. 6. With no foxes to eat them, the rabbits would increase; more rabbits would eat more grass, so the grass would decrease.\nDraw a Pond Food Web: A complete web has at least six living things with arrows pointing to the eater, for example algae → tadpole, algae → minnow, tadpole → dragonfly, mosquito → dragonfly, minnow → heron, tadpole (or frog) → heron, and dead matter → bacteria. Algae and cattails are labeled producers; tadpoles, minnows, mosquitoes, dragonflies and herons are consumers; bacteria are decomposers. The spoken explanation follows one path from the sun or a producer to a top consumer.\nShould Willow Pond Get Bass?: Either opinion can earn full credit. Strong \"no\" reasons: bass eat minnows, frogs, tadpoles and dragonfly larvae; the ranger says they could eat most of the minnows in two or three years; minnows and dragonfly larvae eat mosquito larvae, so fewer of them means more mosquitoes, which are already a problem; herons and kingfishers would lose food; nothing in the pond eats full-grown bass. Strong \"yes\" reasons: visitors for the town and a place for families to fish; possible conditions, such as adding fewer bass or watching the minnow numbers. The food-web reason must show at least two steps (bass eat minnows → fewer minnows eat mosquito larvae → more mosquitoes).\nFood Web Check: 1. Grasses and clover; they soak up sunlight to make their own food. 2. Example: clover → mouse → snake → hawk, or grass → grasshopper → snake → hawk. 3. The mouse got energy from clover leaves, seeds or grasshoppers; the grasshoppers got it from grass; the plants got it from the sun. 4. They are decomposers: they break down dead leaves, seeds and animals and return the matter to the soil, where plant roots take it up. Without them, dead things would pile up and the plants would run short of minerals and grow less. 5. Grasshoppers eat grass; when most of them died, much less grass was eaten, so it grew taller. 6. Mice lost some of their food, so there may have been fewer mice or they ate more clover and seeds; snakes also lost grasshoppers and may have had fewer mice to eat, so their numbers might drop too.\nScoring tip: on questions 5 and 6, a correct prediction with no \"because\" is Developing on reasoning; tracing two links in the web is Proficient.",
  "id": "u4-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Ecosystems and Food Webs",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{
  "body": "Every ecosystem runs on energy from the sun.

- Producers, like plants and algae, use sunlight, air and water to make their own food.

files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students explain how energy and matter move among producers, consumers and decomposers, using cause and effect (RI.5.3, RI.5.4).
- Students present a food web as a visual display and explain one path of energy aloud, in a logical order (SL.5.4, SL.5.5).
- Students write an opinion piece about a change to an ecosystem, supported with facts from a text (W.5.1, W.5.9).
- Students quote accurately from an informational text when explaining what it says (RI.5.1).

MATERIALS
- Cards with pictures of pond and meadow living things, and yarn to connect them into a web
- Drawing paper, colored pencils, and devices to record explanations
- Willow Pond: Facts for the Town Meeting (in the opinion assignment), printed or on tablets
- Optional: a rotting log or leaf litter in a sealed clear container to observe decomposers over the unit

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Who Eats Whom? Lesson: Energy Moves Through an Ecosystem. Discuss question 2: most of a tree comes from air and water, a surprise for many students.
Day 2: Yarn web game: each student holds a card; pass yarn from food to eater. Remove one card (cut its strands) and see what is affected. Assignment: Draw a Pond Food Web, started in class.
Day 3: Finish and record the pond food web explanations. Read the Willow Pond fact sheet together and list facts for and against the bass.
Day 4: Assignment: Should Willow Pond Get Bass? Students plan with a two-column organizer, then write. Partners check that one reason explains the food web step by step.
Day 5: Assessment: Food Web Check. Students read and answer on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a partly drawn food web with the living things placed and let students add the arrows and labels. Offer an opinion organizer with boxes for two reasons and two facts.
- Support: read the meadow passage aloud to any student whose reading plan allows it.
- Stretch: ask students to argue the other side of the bass question in one paragraph and then rebut it.
- Multilingual learners: teach the arrow as "is eaten by" with a gesture. Post producer, consumer, decomposer, predator and prey with pictures, and let students rehearse the food web explanation with a partner first.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are studying food webs: who eats whom, and how the sun's energy moves from plants to animals. Here is a fun fact to ask your child about: most of a tree's wood comes from the air, not the soil! This week your child is also writing an opinion about whether a town should add fish to a pond. Ask what they decided, and what evidence convinced them.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Ecosystems and Food Webs",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u5-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Our Star and the Night Sky: 1. It is much closer to us than any other star (about 150 million kilometers, while the next star's light takes more than four years to reach us); it is not the biggest or brightest star in space. 2. Earth spins: \"It turns once every 24 hours, carrying us from the sunny side into the dark side and back again.\" 3. In the early morning the sun is low in the sky, so shadows are long; around noon the sun is highest, so shadows are shortest. 4. As Earth moves along its orbit, the night side faces different parts of space; in winter it faces Orion in the evening, and in summer it faces another direction. 5. Down, toward the center of Earth, because Earth's gravity pulls everything toward the planet's center, wherever you are. 6. 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes.\nShadow Tracker: A fair investigation keeps the same stick in the same place and measures the same way each time. Data list the time, the length in centimeters and the direction. Typical results: long shadows pointing west in the morning, the shortest shadow around midday pointing north (in the Northern Hemisphere), and long shadows pointing east in the afternoon, so the graphed points fall and then rise. The longest shadow is written in meters (for example, 145 cm = 1.45 m). The explanation says that as Earth spins, the sun's position in our sky changes, which changes the length and direction of the shadow.\nEarth and Space Check: A strong explanation says: (1) the sun seems to move across the sky because Earth spins once every 24 hours, so we turn toward the sun in the morning and away from it at night; (2) shadows change because, as Earth spins, the sun is low in the morning and evening (long shadows) and high around noon (short shadows), and shadows point away from the sun; (3) we see different stars in different seasons because Earth orbits the sun once a year, so at night our side faces different parts of space; (4) the sun looks brighter than other stars because it is much closer to Earth, not because it is the biggest star.\nScoring tip: an answer that says \"the sun moves around the Earth\" is Beginning on science for that part; reward explanations that name what Earth is doing.",
  "id": "u5-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Earth and Space",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

As we move, the night side of Earth faces different parts of space, so we see different stars in different seasons.\n\nAnd wherever you stand on Earth, gravity pulls you down, toward Earth's center.",

files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students explain, from an informational text, how Earth's spin and orbit cause day and night, changing shadows and seasonal star patterns, and which way gravity pulls (RI.5.1, RI.5.3).
- Students convert hours to minutes and centimeters to meters (5.MD.A.1).
- Students carry out a shadow investigation, record data and graph it as points on a coordinate grid (W.5.7, W.5.8, 5.G.A.2).
- Students write an informative explanation that states causes, for a younger audience (W.5.2, W.5.4).

MATERIALS
- A meter stick or a straight stick, chalk, a ruler or tape measure in centimeters, a compass (or the directions marked on the playground)
- A lamp without a shade and a globe, or a ball on a pencil, for modeling Earth's spin
- Star maps of a winter and a summer evening sky (one with Orion, one without)
- Grid paper for graphing

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Our Place in Space. Model day and night: turn the globe in front of the lamp and find your city as it moves into the light. Lesson: Our Star and the Night Sky, read in pairs.
Day 2: Assignment: Shadow Tracker. Set up the sticks in the morning and measure the shadow every hour (or as often as the schedule allows), marking its tip with chalk. Indoor option on a cloudy day: a flashlight moved in an arc over a pencil.
Day 3: Graph the shadow data. Mini-lesson on plotting points and converting centimeters to meters. Students write conclusions.
Day 4: Model the orbit: students walk the globe in a circle around the lamp with star posters on the walls, and notice which posters the night side faces in each season. Discuss gravity with a globe and small figures standing in different countries.
Day 5: Assessment: Earth and Space Check. Students write on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a shadow data table with the times filled in and a graph with the axes labeled and numbered. Offer the frames from the lesson for the assessment.
- Support: let students act out spin and orbit with a partner before they write.
- Stretch: ask students to predict how the noon shadow would differ in winter and summer, and test the idea with the lamp model.
- Multilingual learners: teach spin, orbit, rise, set, shadow and gravity with gestures and pictures. Let students explain the globe model aloud before writing.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning why the sun seems to move across the sky (Earth is spinning!), why shadows change during the day, and why we see different stars in different seasons. Try this at home: on a sunny day, have your child stand in the same spot in the morning and again at lunch time, and compare the length of their shadow. On a clear evening, look for a bright group of stars together and see whether it is still there in a few months.",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Earth and Space",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "How Engineers Solve Problems: 1. Criteria are what a good design must do; constraints are the limits you must work within. Criteria: keep milk cold for at least four hours, or fit in a backpack. Constraints: no more than $5 per design, only materials from the classroom bin, or two class periods to build. 2. A first model of a design; engineers build one to test whether the idea works and to find what to improve. 3. So they would know which change made the difference; if they changed two things, they could not tell which one helped. 4. Sequence of steps: first, next, then, with each step of the design process in order; or problem and solution: warm milk is the problem and the improved box is the solution. Either is correct with evidence. 5. The failed test showed them what was wrong (heat getting in through the open top), so they knew what to change. 6. Example criteria: holds a full backpack without breaking; lets a student hang and remove a backpack easily. Example constraints: no holes in the wall, a set cost or set materials, a set size or build time.\nKeep It Cold: Design an Ice Keeper: A fair test uses ice cubes of the same size, the same place and the same 60 minutes, with an unprotected cube for comparison. Data are in grams, with ice melted = mass at start − mass after 60 minutes. Typical results: insulated designs (foam, felt, bubble wrap, a lid) let much less ice melt than the unprotected cube. A strong improvement changes one thing (for example, adding a lid or a second layer) and explains that it slows heat from getting in.\nDesign Check: Which Cooler Should We Buy?: The best choice is Cooler A, the only one that meets every criterion and constraint: 6 hours (at least 5), $35 (no more than $40), and 1.8 kg (2 kg or less). Cooler B kept the milk cold the longest (9 hours) but costs $55, over the $40 limit, and its mass is 2,500 g = 2.5 kg, more than 2 kg. Cooler C is cheap ($20) and light (900 g = 0.9 kg) but kept the milk cold for only 3 hours, less than 5, and its zipper broke. Reasonable improvements for Cooler A: thicker insulation or a better-sealing lid, tested one change at a time.\nScoring tip: a student who chooses B or C can still earn Proficient on evidence if the data are used correctly, but scores Beginning or Developing on criteria for not checking a constraint the choice breaks.",

{
  "body": "Engineers solve problems by designing things.

The engineering design process:
1. Define the problem. What must the design do (the criteria)? What limits do you have, like cost, time or materials (the constraints)?
2. Brainstorm many ideas, then pick one.
3. Build a model, called a prototype.
4. Test it fairly and record data.
5. Improve it, changing one thing at a time, and test again.

A design that fails is not the end. It gives you data about what to change. In this unit we will design something that keeps an ice cube from melting.",

{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students explain the steps of the engineering design process and how a text is organized, and explain the words criteria, constraints and prototype from context (RI.5.3, RI.5.4, RI.5.5).
- Students design, build and fairly test a solution, record data with units and improve it based on the data (W.5.7, W.5.8).
- Students write an opinion that chooses a design by checking test data against criteria and constraints, converting grams to kilograms where needed (W.5.1, W.5.9, 5.MD.A.1).

MATERIALS
- Ice cubes of the same size, paper cups, a scale in grams, a timer, paper towels
- A class bin of materials: foil, felt, cotton balls, bubble wrap, newspaper, foam pieces, plastic wrap, rubber bands, tape
- Cooler Test Results (in the assessment), printed or on tablets
- Chart paper with the five steps of the design process

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Think Like an Engineer. Lesson: How Engineers Solve Problems. Make a class chart of criteria and constraints for the ice keeper.
Day 2: Assignment: Keep It Cold. Teams brainstorm, sketch and pick a design, then build their prototype within the constraints.
Day 3: Test: weigh each ice cube, put it in its keeper (and one unprotected cube on a plate), wait 60 minutes, weigh what is left and subtract. Record the data.
Day 4: Share results in a gallery walk. Each team makes one improvement, changing one thing, and retests if time allows. Students finish the analysis. Practice converting grams to kilograms.
Day 5: Assessment: Design Check. Students read the test results and write on their own.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a design planner with boxes for criteria, constraints, sketch and materials, and a data table with the subtraction column set up. Model one gram-to-kilogram conversion before the assessment.
- Support: offer a checklist table (Cooler, 5 hours?, $40 or less?, 2 kg or less?) for students to fill before they write.
- Stretch: ask students to calculate the cost per hour of cold milk for each cooler and decide whether it changes their choice.
- Multilingual learners: post criteria, constraints, prototype, test and improve with icons. Let teams present their design with a labeled sketch before writing.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our scientists are now engineers! This week your child's team is designing a container that keeps an ice cube from melting, using only classroom materials. Ask your child what their design's criteria (what it must do) and constraints (its limits) were, and what they changed after their first test. Engineers learn as much from what fails as from what works.",

  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Engineering Design",

}
